About: Glancing Collision — Two Unknowns, One Law Each

Source

Topic
Two-dimensional elastic collision (glancing)
Concept
Momentum in 2D is two equations; with elastic energy that's three — one short of fixing the outcome. The missing piece is how off-centre the hit was.
The one thing to notice
With equal masses the two outgoing velocities are always exactly 90° apart. The right angle collapses the moment masses differ.
Audience
JEE (NCERT Class 11–12)

Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict the between-angle

Two identical billiard balls: ball 1 rolls in along the dashed line; ball 2 sits at rest. You will vary how off-centre the hit is — from grazing to nearly head-on.

Before you touch anything: what happens to the angle between the two outgoing paths as the hit goes from grazing to head-on?

2 · Sweep the star control

Press ▶ Play, then drag the How head-on slider from grazing to nearly head-on and back. Watch the arc between the two outgoing paths and its reading.

Every setting, every mass-equal collision: the arc reads 90°. The two speeds change, the two directions change — but their separation does not.

3 · Why can't momentum alone give you the answer?

You have two unknowns per ball after the collision (a speed and a direction), so four unknowns total. Momentum is conserved in x and in y separately. Energy is conserved (elastic). That's three equations, four unknowns.

What supplies the fourth piece of information?

4 · Break the symmetry

Now change one of the masses. Drag m₁ or m₂ away from equal and watch the between-angle badge.

The 90° collapses the instant the masses differ. That right angle was a special property of equal-mass elastic collisions — not a general truth about 2D collisions. Try m₁ = 3 kg, m₂ = 1 kg with a moderate off-centre hit: the angle drops well below 90°.

5 · The take-away

In one dimension, momentum + elastic energy fixes both outgoing velocities. In two dimensions momentum is two equations, elastic energy is a third, and you are still one short — the impact parameter supplies the fourth piece.

The signature result: with equal masses the algebra collapses to exactly 90° between the outgoing paths, at every off-centre setting — and it fails as soon as the masses differ.

01

At a glance

A ball rolls in along a dashed line and strikes a second ball that is at rest. The balls leave along two new paths, and you choose how head-on the hit is and how heavy each ball is.

What you'll learn

  • Why momentum and energy conservation alone cannot fix a collision in two dimensions.
  • How the outgoing paths depend on how head-on the hit is.
  • How the masses of the two balls enter the result.
Before the hit: ball 1 on the dashed axis, ball 2 at rest at the dot.

What's on screen

  • Balls: ball 1 (blue, m₁) and ball 2 (pink, m₂). Their size grows a little with mass and is only a hint.
  • Dashed axis with the dot where the balls meet, and a fading trail behind each ball.
  • Arc and badge that appear at the hit, with the angle between the two outgoing velocities.
See itPress Play and watch ball 1 roll in. Watch for: ball 1 travelling along the dashed axis at 5 m/s and reaching the dot, where ball 2 waits, after 0.6 s.

03

Three equations are not enough to fix a collision in two dimensions

After the hit each ball has a speed and a direction, so there are four unknowns: v₁′, θ₁, v₂′ and θ₂. The angles are measured from the incoming line. Momentum is a vector, so it gives one equation along x and one along y:

m₁u = m₁v₁′ cos θ₁ + m₂v₂′ cos θ₂
0 = m₁v₁′ sin θ₁ − m₂v₂′ sin θ₂
Momentum along the incoming line (x) and across it (y).

An elastic collision keeps the kinetic energy, ½m₁u² = ½m₁v₁′² + ½m₂v₂′², which is a third equation. Three equations for four unknowns leave one unknown free. In one dimension two unknown velocities and two equations are enough, so the shortfall comes from the extra direction.

See itPress Play and look at what the sim reports after the hit. Watch for: two outgoing speeds in the Final speeds panel, 2.94 and 4.05 m/s, and two outgoing directions on the table.
04

How head-on supplies the missing piece

The fourth piece is geometry: a head-on hit sends ball 1 back, and a grazing hit barely turns it. Momentum and energy cannot say which hit happened, so the sim gives it a slider.

In the centre-of-mass frame an elastic collision keeps both speeds and only turns the directions through an angle θCM. The slider sets it:

θCM = π × (How head-on)
Near 0 the balls barely turn, near 180° (π) ball 1 turns straight back in the centre-of-mass frame.

At 0.60, θCM = 108°. With any masses, ball 2 then leaves 90° − θCM/2 = 36° below the incoming line. For real hard balls the offset of the line from ball 2's centre is b = d cos(θCM/2), with d the sum of the radii, so b = 0.59d here. The sim does not draw this offset. Ball 1 always travels the dashed axis.

See itPress Play with How head-on at the grazing end, 0.05. Watch for: ball 1 hardly turning, at 4.98 m/s, while ball 2 creeps away at 0.39 m/s nearly at right angles.
05

Equal masses always leave at right angles

Take m₁ = m₂ with ball 2 at rest. The mass cancels from momentum conservation, and energy conservation loses its ½m:

u⃗ = v⃗₁′ + v⃗₂′   and   u² = v₁′² + v₂′²
Squaring the first and using the second gives v⃗₁′ · v⃗₂′ = 0.

A zero dot product means the two velocities are perpendicular, so θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°. This holds at every How head-on setting, as long as both balls move. At 0.60 ball 1 leaves at 2.94 m/s, 54° above the incoming line, and ball 2 at 4.05 m/s, 36° below it. Check: 2.94² + 4.05² = 25 = 5².

See itPress Play with both masses at 1.0 kg and How head-on at 0.60. Watch for: the green badge between the two paths reading 90.0°.
06

Unequal masses break the right angle

Without m₁ = m₂, the same steps give a dot product that depends on the masses:

v⃗₁′ · v⃗₂′ = (m₁ − m₂) v₂′² / (2m₁)
For an elastic collision with ball 2 initially at rest.

A heavier incoming ball (m₁ > m₂) makes the dot product positive, so the paths are less than 90° apart. A lighter one (m₁ < m₂) makes it negative, so they are more than 90° apart. Only ball 1's direction changes with the masses, since ball 2 still leaves at 36° below the line at 0.60.

At 0.60, m₁ = 3 kg and m₂ = 1 kg give 55.5°. Swapping them, m₁ = 1 kg and m₂ = 3 kg, gives 124.5°.

See itPress Play with a heavy ball 1, m₁ = 3 kg and m₂ = 1 kg. Watch for: the amber badge reading 55.5°, well below 90°.
See itNow press Play with a light ball 1, m₁ = 1 kg and m₂ = 3 kg. Watch for: the badge reading 124.5°, above 90°.
07

The two speeds trade off as the hit gets more head-on

For equal masses the right angle makes the two speeds the shorter sides of a right triangle whose long side is u:

v₁′ = u cos(θCM/2)   v₂′ = u sin(θCM/2)
Equal masses, ball 2 initially at rest.

A grazing hit leaves ball 1 almost untouched, and a head-on hit passes almost all of ball 1's motion to ball 2. At 0.05 the speeds are 4.98 and 0.39 m/s. At 0.98 they are 0.16 and 5.00 m/s. The kinetic energy is split in the ratio cos² : sin² of θCM/2, and its total never changes.

The Final speeds panel lists both speeds and the fixed incoming 5.00 m/s.

See itPress Play with How head-on near the head-on end, 0.98. Watch for: ball 1 nearly stopping at 0.16 m/s while ball 2 leaves at 5.00 m/s, still 90° apart.
08

Where it matters

  • Billiards. A cue ball that hits a stationary object ball without spin leaves at about 90° to it. Spin, friction and a small loss of energy shift this a little.
  • Particle tracks. A slow proton hitting a proton at rest leaves a V of two tracks at 90° in a cloud or bubble chamber. At relativistic speeds the angle is smaller.
  • Neutron moderators. A neutron hitting a hydrogen nucleus, of almost equal mass, can give up most or all of its energy in one hit.
09

Summary

In one line. A glancing collision of two balls obeys momentum and energy conservation, and the sim lets you change the hit and the masses and read the outgoing paths.

Key points

  • Momentum in 2D gives two equations and elastic energy a third, one short of four unknowns.
  • How head-on supplies the fourth: θCM = π × the slider.
  • Equal masses give exactly 90°. A heavier ball 1 gives less, and a lighter one gives more.

Common mix-ups

"The 90° rule holds for every collision." It needs an elastic hit, equal masses and a target at rest.
"Energy is lost when the balls fly off at an angle." The collision is elastic, so the total kinetic energy is the same before and after.

Things to try on your own

  • With equal masses, sweep How head-on from 0.05 to 0.98 and note what stays fixed.
  • Set m₁ = 0.5 kg and m₂ = 4 kg and find which way ball 1 goes.
